meta.title: AI Governance Compass
meta.description: Side-by-side comparison of the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and Kenya's Data Protection Act across seven governance dimensions.

frameworks.name: Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI
India AI Governance Guidelines
frameworks.type: Non-binding guidance + adjacent binding data law

frameworks.name: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI

entries.summary: Four-tier risk model: unacceptable, high, limited, minimal.
No fixed tiers; context-specific risk profiling via the Map function.
entries.note: Clause reference not yet independently re-verified against the NIST AI RMF 1.0 PDF. Verify Map function sub-category numbering before treating as final.

entries.summary: Management-system risk assessment plus AI system impact assessment.
entries.note: ISO/IEC 42001 full text is paywalled; clause numbers sourced from secondary summaries and not checked against the purchased standard. Flag as lower-confidence until verified against the official text.

entries.summary: No AI-specific risk tiers; risk is framed around high-risk personal data processing.
Directly applicable EU regulation with phased compliance deadlines.
Voluntary guidance; may become binding through contracts or procurement.
Certifiable standard; enforceable only via audit and certification, not law.
Binding national statute supervised by the Data Commissioner (ODPC).
High-risk systems require representative, error-examined training, validation and testing data.
Recommends provenance, representativeness and drift-monitoring practices.
Annex A controls for data quality, provenance and lifecycle handling.
Lawful basis and purpose-limitation/minimisation rules for personal data; data localisation is addressed separately.
entries.note: Corrected from earlier draft: localisation is governed by Sec. 50, not Sec. 25/30. Kept as a separate citation to avoid overstating what 25/30 cover.

entries.summary: Users must be told they are interacting with AI; synthetic/manipulated media must be labelled.
Treats transparency as a trustworthiness characteristic rather than a standalone duty.
Requires documented information be made available to users and affected parties.
Data subjects must be informed of processing purposes and, for automated decisions, the logic involved.
High-risk systems must be designed to allow effective human oversight and intervention.
Encourages defined human-AI configurations and override pathways.
Defines roles, responsibilities and human control points within the AI management system.
Right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that produces legal or similarly significant effects.
Technical documentation plus automatic event logging for traceability.
Suggests model and use-case documentation; no prescribed template.
Extensive documented-information and internal audit trail obligations.
Data protection impact assessments and processing records required for high-risk processing.
Fines up to EUR 35m or 7% of global turnover, whichever is higher, for prohibited-practice breaches (Art. 5); lower tiers (up to EUR 15m/3% and EUR 7.5m/1%) apply to other operator obligations.
No penalties; accountability rests entirely on the adopting organisation.
Non-conformity leads to loss or denial of certification rather than legal sanction.
Administrative fines up to KES 5m or 1% of annual turnover, whichever is lower.
entries.note: Corrected from earlier draft: the Act specifies 'whichever is lower', not an unqualified KES 5m/1% cap. A 2025 Amendment Bill would flip this to 'whichever is higher' but is not yet law — do not conflate the two. Removed unverified 'plus compensation' claim pending confirmation of the specific compensation provision.

entries.summary: Two-tier approach: 'high-impact AI' (defined sectors affecting life, safety, fundamental rights) and 'high-performance AI' (compute-threshold based, ~10^26 FLOPs).
entries.note: Compute threshold and high-impact/high-performance distinction confirmed via multiple 2026 legal-practitioner summaries of Act No. 20676; not yet cross-checked against the official Korean statutory text directly.

entries.summary: Binding statute (Act No. 20676), promulgated Jan 2025, in force from 22 Jan 2026, with a one-year grace period before fines/corrective orders are actively enforced.
Requires risk management and safety measures for AI trained on large-scale data; ties into Korea's PIPA (data protection law) for personal-data-specific rules.
Operators of generative or high-impact AI must notify users in advance that they are interacting with AI, and label AI-generated output where it could be mistaken for human-made content.
High-impact AI operators must implement risk-management systems including human oversight mechanisms as part of lifecycle governance.
Impact assessments and compliance documentation required for high-impact AI; foreign operators without a Korean presence must appoint a domestic representative.

Administrative fines and corrective orders apply, but were deferred for at least one year from the Jan 2026 effective date except in cases of serious social harm (e.g. loss of life, human-rights violations).
No formal risk tiers; instead a 'classified and graded supervision' concept, with extra security-assessment/filing duties for services with 'public opinion or social mobilisation capacity.'

Binding administrative regulation (not a National People's Congress law); part of a layered stack alongside the Algorithm Recommendation Provisions and Deep Synthesis Provisions. In force since 15 Aug 2023; applies extraterritorially to services offered to the Chinese public.

Providers must ensure training data is lawfully sourced and take measures to improve training data quality; separately governed alongside China's Data Security Law and Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL).
AI-generated content must be labelled (visible and machine-readable labels), reinforced by the separate 2025 Measures for Labelling AI-Generated and Synthetic Content.
entries.sourceClause: Deep Synthesis Provisions + Labelling Measures (eff. 1 Sept 2025)

entries.summary: No explicit standalone human-oversight article; content moderation and provider accountability obligations function as a substitute oversight mechanism.
Algorithm filing with the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) is required before public launch for qualifying services; as of early 2026, hundreds of services had completed filing.
No standalone penalty schedule in the Measures themselves; violations are enforced through the existing statutory ladder under the Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, and PIPL.
No fixed risk tiers; requires parties to adopt risk and impact-assessment measures for AI systems affecting human rights, democracy, and the rule of law, left to domestic implementation.

The first legally binding international treaty on AI; opened for signature in Sept 2024, binding only on states that ratify it (open to non-Council-of-Europe states, e.g. the US, Canada were signatories).
General obligation that data processing within the AI lifecycle respects data protection law of each party; does not itself set detailed data-governance rules.
Requires parties to ensure adequate transparency regarding AI systems in ways that support affected persons' ability to contest decisions.
Requires accountability and human oversight mechanisms proportionate to the risks posed by AI systems throughout their lifecycle.
Framework-level obligation only; leaves specific documentation and record-keeping requirements to each party's domestic implementing legislation.
No supranational fines; enforcement and penalties are left to each ratifying party's domestic law, with treaty-level oversight through a Conference of the Parties.

No binding AI-specific risk classification currently in force. The proposed AIDA's 'high-impact AI system' concept died with the bill in Jan 2025; risk is instead addressed piecemeal through privacy and human-rights law.
entries.sourceClause: n/a — AIDA (Bill C-27) did not pass
entries.note: AIDA died on the order paper when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025 and has not been reintroduced as of mid-2026. This entry reflects that Canada currently has no binding AI-specific statute, correcting the assumption that AIDA is in force.

entries.summary: No comprehensive federal AI law in force. AI-adjacent obligations arise instead from PIPEDA (federal privacy law), Quebec's Law 25, the binding federal Directive on Automated Decision-Making for government institutions, and a voluntary Code of Conduct for Generative AI.
Personal-data processing by AI systems is governed by PIPEDA federally and Quebec's Law 25 provincially; no AI-specific data-governance statute exists.

The voluntary Code of Conduct for Generative AI encourages transparency (e.g. content labelling) but is non-binding; the binding federal Directive on Automated Decision-Making imposes transparency duties only on federal government institutions.
entries.sourceClause: Voluntary Code of Conduct for Generative AI; Directive on ADM

entries.summary: The Directive on Automated Decision-Making requires proportional human oversight for federal government ADM systems; no equivalent binding requirement exists for the private sector.
Algorithmic impact assessments are mandatory for federal government ADM systems under the Directive; no binding private-sector documentation requirement currently exists.
No AI-specific penalty regime in force. Enforcement runs through PIPEDA, provincial privacy law, and human-rights law; a 2026 successor to AIDA has been signalled but not yet tabled.

Deliberately avoids fixed statutory risk tiers; instead applies five cross-sectoral principles (safety, transparency, fairness, accountability, contestability) enforced by existing sectoral regulators.
Non-statutory, principles-based policy framework; no dedicated UK AI Act exists. Existing sectoral regulators (ICO, FCA, MHRA, etc.) apply the principles within their own statutory powers.
No AI-specific data-governance statute; personal-data processing by AI systems falls under the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018, enforced by the ICO.
Transparency is one of the five cross-sectoral principles; implementation and enforcement is delegated to individual regulators rather than set out in a single binding transparency duty.
Accountability and contestability principles imply human-oversight expectations, but no single statutory human-oversight requirement applies across sectors.
No centralised documentation mandate; individual regulators may impose sector-specific record-keeping requirements under their existing statutory powers.
No AI-specific penalty regime; enforcement relies entirely on existing sectoral regulators' own powers (e.g. ICO fines under UK GDPR, FCA enforcement in financial services).
Voluntary risk-based guidance encouraging organisations to assess AI risk by considering probability and severity of harm; not a mandatory tiering scheme.
Entirely voluntary guidance issued by Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority and Personal Data Protection Commission; not legally binding.
Recommends internal governance structures for data management in AI systems; binding data rules instead come from Singapore's separate Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA).
entries.sourceClause: Model AI Governance Framework, 2nd Ed.; PDPA (binding, separate statute)

entries.summary: Recommends proactive communication with users about AI use and its role in decision-making, as voluntary best practice rather than a legal duty.
Recommends a human-in-the-loop, human-out-of-the-loop, or human-over-the-loop model depending on risk level, as voluntary guidance.
Encourages internal documentation of AI decision-making processes; reinforced by companion tools like AI Verify, a voluntary AI governance testing framework.
entries.sourceClause: Model AI Governance Framework, 2nd Ed.; AI Verify

entries.summary: No penalties under the Framework itself; only Singapore's separate binding PDPA carries enforceable data-protection penalties.
entries.sourceClause: n/a — PDPA is the binding statute

entries.summary: Proposed three-tier risk model: excessive risk (prohibited), high risk, and non-high/non-excessive risk, closely modelled on the EU AI Act.

Not yet law. Approved by the Federal Senate on 10 Dec 2024; forwarded to the Chamber of Deputies in March 2025, where it remained under committee review as of mid-2026 with no fixed timeline for a floor vote.
entries.note: Status confirmed current as of this dataset's last-updated date; the bill's content may still change materially before enactment.

entries.summary: Would align closely with Brazil's existing General Data Protection Law (LGPD, Law No. 13,709/2018), which already applies to personal-data processing by AI systems regardless of the bill's outcome.
Proposed bill would require AI systems to be understandable and auditable, with disclosure obligations for high-risk and generative/general-purpose systems.
Proposed bill includes human oversight and impact-assessment requirements for high-risk systems, modelled on the EU AI Act's approach.
Would require governance documentation and, for generative/general-purpose systems, mandatory preliminary risk assessments under the bill's proposed National AI Regulation and Governance System.
Proposed fines of up to BRL 50 million or 2% of a company's gross turnover, enforced by Brazil's national data protection authority (ANPD) acting as AI regulator — not yet in force pending enactment.

No binding AI-specific risk classification; MeitY's advisory guidance encourages voluntary risk assessment, while the binding Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 applies generally to personal-data processing without AI-specific tiers.

No dedicated AI statute currently in force. The DPDP Act, 2023 is binding for personal data generally; AI-specific rules exist only as non-binding advisories from India's Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY).
Personal-data processing (including by AI systems) is governed by the binding DPDP Act, 2023; no separate AI-specific data-governance statute exists.
MeitY's non-binding AI advisory recommends labelling of AI-generated content and disclosure of known limitations; not a statutory requirement.
No binding human-oversight requirement specific to AI; general principles are addressed only through non-binding advisory guidance.
No binding AI-specific documentation mandate; DPDP Act obligations apply to personal-data records generally, not to AI system documentation specifically.
No AI-specific penalty regime; enforcement is limited to DPDP Act penalties for personal-data violations (which can reach up to INR 250 crore per instance), with no equivalent for AI-specific harms.
Sets high-level continental principles rather than a binding risk taxonomy; leaves specific risk classification to individual African Union member states.
A non-binding continental strategy adopted by the African Union in July 2024, intended to guide (not compel) member-state AI policy and regional harmonisation.
Emphasises data sovereignty and cross-border data governance harmonisation across AU member states as a strategic priority, without imposing binding rules itself.
Encourages transparency and public trust in AI as a strategic pillar, left to member states to implement through domestic policy.
References human-centred AI and human rights protection as guiding principles, without prescribing specific oversight mechanisms.
No documentation mandate at the continental level; the strategy calls for member states to build national AI governance capacity, which may include documentation regimes.
No enforcement mechanism at the continental level; the strategy is aspirational and relies entirely on voluntary member-state adoption and domestic legislation.
Primarily an industrial and innovation strategy rather than a risk-based governance instrument; no binding AI-specific risk tiers.
A non-binding national strategy setting goals for AI adoption and leadership by 2031; not itself a law, though the UAE has separately issued sector-specific and emirate-level AI/data regulations.
References data as a strategic national asset and encourages responsible data governance, with specific binding rules left to instruments like the UAE's federal and free-zone data protection laws.
Encourages public trust and ethical AI adoption as strategic goals, without a specific binding transparency obligation.
References ethical and responsible AI principles at a high level; specific human-oversight mechanisms are not detailed in the strategy itself.
No documentation mandate at the strategy level; implementation is delegated to sector regulators and government entities executing the strategy's programmes.
No enforcement mechanism within the strategy itself; it functions as a policy roadmap rather than an enforceable regulatory instrument.
Encourages risk-proportionate approaches to AI governance as a general principle, without prescribing a specific risk taxonomy; widely referenced by binding frameworks like the EU AI Act.

Non-binding intergovernmental principles adopted by OECD members and adherent non-member countries in 2019 and updated in 2024; the first intergovernmental AI standard, though not legally enforceable.
Calls for AI systems to respect the rule of law, human rights, and democratic values, including data privacy, without setting specific binding data-governance rules.
Transparency and explainability are one of the five core OECD AI Principles, calling for meaningful information disclosure to enable people to understand AI-based outcomes.
Robustness, security, and safety principle calls for mechanisms enabling human oversight where appropriate, without prescribing specific mechanisms.
No documentation mandate; the Principles are implemented through voluntary adoption and the OECD's AI Policy Observatory tracking member-state implementation.
No enforcement mechanism; accountability rests entirely on adhering countries' own domestic implementation and law-making.
Recommends ethical impact assessments proportionate to the severity of potential harm, without setting a fixed risk taxonomy.
entries.sourceClause: Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, 2021

entries.summary: Non-binding recommendation adopted by all 193 UNESCO member states in November 2021; the first global normative instrument on AI ethics, but not legally enforceable.
entries.sourceClause: Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, 2021

entries.summary: Calls for data governance approaches that protect privacy and ensure data quality throughout the AI lifecycle, as an ethical value rather than a binding rule.
entries.sourceClause: Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, 2021

entries.summary: Transparency and explainability are named as core ethical values, with a recommendation that member states promote them through domestic policy.
entries.sourceClause: Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, 2021

entries.summary: Human oversight and determination are named as core values, emphasising that final decisions with significant impact should retain human involvement.
entries.sourceClause: Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, 2021

entries.summary: Encourages member states to establish AI ethical impact assessment processes and readiness assessment methodologies; UNESCO provides voluntary self-assessment tools rather than mandating documentation itself.
entries.sourceClause: Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, 2021

entries.summary: No enforcement mechanism; implementation is monitored voluntarily through member states' periodic reporting to UNESCO.
entries.sourceClause: Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, 2021

divergences.title: Agentic AI is under-addressed across all frameworks
divergences.description: None of the primary frameworks fully address multi-agent orchestration or autonomous decision delegation, leaving accountability for chained actions unresolved.

divergences.title: Risk is classified by product tier vs. by context
divergences.description: The EU AI Act fixes risk categories in law, while NIST and ISO expect organisations to derive risk from deployment context — the same system can be 'high-risk' in one regime and unclassified in another.

divergences.title: Enforcement teeth vary by orders of magnitude
divergences.description: Turnover-based fines in the EU and Kenya sit alongside purely reputational consequences under NIST and certification loss under ISO, creating uneven compliance incentives for multinational deployers.

divergences.title: Data-protection law carries AI duties by proxy
divergences.description: Kenya's DPA governs AI indirectly through personal-data rules, so systems that do not process personal data fall outside its oversight entirely — a gap AI-specific frameworks attempt to close.

divergences.title: Several major economies still have no binding AI-specific law
divergences.description: Canada's AIDA died in Parliament in Jan 2025, Brazil's PL 2338/2023 remains pending years after Senate approval, and India relies on non-binding advisories — all three fall back on general-purpose data protection law rather than AI-specific statutes, unlike the EU, South Korea, or China.

divergences.title: "Regulation" means very different things by jurisdiction
divergences.description: China governs AI through binding administrative measures issued by regulators (not a parliamentary AI law), the EU and South Korea have full legislative AI statutes, the Council of Europe has a binding international treaty, while the AU, UAE, OECD and UNESCO instruments are strategic or aspirational with no enforcement teeth — comparing them on a single "binding vs voluntary" axis understates how differently each actually operates.

divergences.title: The only binding global AI treaty has an open ratification gap
divergences.description: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI is the first legally binding international AI treaty and was opened to non-European signatories, but it binds only states that ratify it — leaving a structural gap versus regional laws like the EU AI Act that apply automatically and extraterritorially to anyone serving that market.
